title: A Practical Guide to Cloudflare's New cf CLI
summary: Get started with Cloudflare cf CLI: install and authenticate, manage API resources, configure and deploy Workers, and migrate projects from Wrangler safely.
body_markdown:
cf is Cloudflare’s command-line tool for the entire Cloudflare API. It launched in open beta on 28 September 2026, and you install it with` npm i -g cf` on Node.js 22.18 or later.


If you deploy Workers with Wrangler, you probably still open the dashboard for DNS, zones and settings that Wrangler never covered. cf covers both: your account resources and your Worker projects, from one binary. This guide takes you through installing it, reading its output, writing the new TypeScript config, deploying, and moving an existing Worker across. If you need a refresher on Workers first, start with this[beginner’s guide to Cloudflare Workers](https://blog.openreplay.com/beginners-guide-cloudflare-workers/) .


## Key Takeaways


- Install cf with` npm i -g cf` on Node.js 22.18 or later. Bun is not supported, and commands that load cloudflare.config.ts fail under it.
- cf keeps its own credentials, so run` cf auth login` even if Wrangler is already signed in.
- Most commands print their results as JSON on stdout, and status messages go to stderr, so you can pipe output straight into jq.
- Run` cf migrate` before` cf dev` ,` cf build` or` cf deploy` in any project that has a wrangler.toml, wrangler.json or wrangler.jsonc.
- Once the beta ends, Cloudflare plans a final major Wrangler release that points to cf, followed by 18 months of maintenance.


## How Does cf Differ from Wrangler?


cf replaces a CLI that grew one command at a time with one generated from Cloudflare’s OpenAPI schemas. The[launch announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-cf-cli-launch/) puts cf at more than 3,000 API operations, against roughly 280 in Wrangler. The[cf docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cf/wrangler/) count it differently: more than 2,900 commands. Cloudflare built cf with coding agents in mind, but every command works the same way when you type it yourself.


Wrangler cf


Coverage (launch post figures) ~280 operations 3,000+ operations


Config wrangler.toml / wrangler.json / wrangler.jsonc cloudflare.config.ts


Build Wrangler’s bundler (esbuild) Vite by default, or Wrangler’s bundler for migrated projects


Login` wrangler login` Separate` cf auth login`


Status Maintained for 18 months after cf’s beta ends Open beta


The[changelog entry](https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-09-28-cloudflare-cli-beta/) warns that commands, config and Build Output may still change before the stable release.


## How Do You Install cf and Log In?


Install the` cf` package from npm, then authenticate with` cf auth login` . Other tools also install a command called cf, so make sure you have the official package, which links to the[cloudflare/cf repository](https://github.com/cloudflare/cf) .


```text
npm   i   -g   cf
cf   --version


cf   auth   login       # add --no-browser over SSH or in a container
cf   auth   whoami
```


According to the[Get started docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cf/get-started/) , the package gives you the same CLI under two names, cf and cloudflare. If something else on your PATH already answers to cf, call it as cloudflare instead. To log in, cf shows a link and a one-time code, then opens that link in your browser for you to approve. cf stores its own credentials, so a Wrangler login won’t carry over.


In CI, set` CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and` CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` instead. A token set this way[wins over any saved login](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cf/agents/) .


Start with a read-only command:


```text
cf   zones   list
```


## How Do You Read and Filter cf’s JSON Output?


Most cf commands write their results to stdout as JSON, while progress and status messages go to stderr. So you can save results to a file or pipe them into jq with no extra flags.


```text
cf   zones   list   >   zones.json          # results only; status stays on stderr
cf   zones   list   |   jq   .                # inspect the shape
cf   zones   list   |   jq   '  .[].id  '         # print each zone's id
cf   zones   list   --name   example.com    # look up one domain
```


As the[resource management docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cf/get-started/resources/) show,` cf zones list` returns a JSON array in which each zone has an` id` field. Commands that operate inside a zone take` --zone` or its short form` -z` , and accept either a zone ID or a domain name:


```text
cf   dns   records   list   --zone   example.com
cf   dns   records   list   -z   example.com
```


## Find Commands with cf cli search


To find a command, run` cf cli search` with a plain-language description of the task, then open the help for the command it suggests. Per the agents docs,` cf cli search` returns up to five matches as a JSON array, best match first. It searches on your own machine, so you don’t need to be logged in.


```text
cf   cli   search   "  create a DNS record  "
cf   dns   --help
cf   complete   zsh   >>   ~/.zshrc     # shell completion
```


` --help` works at every level of the command tree.


## How Do You Configure Workers with cloudflare.config.ts?


cloudflare.config.ts is cf’s TypeScript configuration file for Workers. It imports` defineConfig` from` cf/config` , default-exports the result, and declares bindings and triggers through typed helpers that your editor can autocomplete. The[programmatic configuration reference](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cf/projects/cloudflare-config/) points out that the file is a normal TypeScript module, so you can use imports, functions, environment variables and async values in it.


The launch post’s first example imports the Worker module with the` with { type: "cf-worker" }` import attribute, then sets` name` ,` entrypoint` and` compatibilityDate` . In the excerpts below,` // ...` stands in for those fields. This trimmed excerpt of the launch post’s` bindings` example passes a function to` defineConfig` so that values can vary by` mode` :


```text
import   {   bindings  ,   defineConfig   }   from   "  cf/config  "  ;


export default   defineConfig  (({   mode   })   =>   ({
worker  :   {
// ...
env  :   {
API_TOKEN  :   bindings  .  secret  (),
DATABASE  :   bindings  .  d1  ({   name  :   `  example-  ${  mode  }  -database  `   }),
UPLOADS  :   bindings  .  r2  ({   name  :   `  example-  ${  mode  }  -uploads  `   }),
JOBS  :   bindings  .  queue  <{   userId  :   string   }>({
name  :   `  example-  ${  mode  }  -jobs  `  ,
}),
AI  :   bindings  .  ai  (),
},
},
}));
```


The full example also uses` bindings.text` ,` bindings.kv` ,` bindings.vectorize` and` bindings.worker` . Triggers live in a single array. This excerpt passes a plain object to` defineConfig` :


```text
import   {   defineConfig  ,   triggers   }   from   "  cf/config  "  ;


export default   defineConfig  ({
worker  :   {
// ...
triggers  :   [
triggers  .  fetch  ({   pattern  :   "  example.com/*  "   }),
triggers  .  scheduled  ({   schedule  :   "  0 * * * *  "   }),
triggers  .  queue  ({   name  :   "  jobs  "  ,   maxBatchSize  :   10   }),
],
},
});
```


The launch post’s version adds a` triggers.email` entry. The reference also lists` triggers.connect` , which covers raw sockets. In the[launch post](https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-cf-cli-launch/) , Cloudflare says it plans to let this file set up zones and DNS too. For now, the default export covers a Worker, Container applications and account settings.


## Init, Deploy and Migrate


Use` cf init` for a new project,` cf deploy` to ship it, and` cf migrate` for an existing Wrangler project.


```text
cf   init   my-worker        # or `cf init .` inside an existing app
cf   deploy
```


` cf init` creates cloudflare.config.ts and vite.config.ts, and in an existing Vite app it installs` @cloudflare/vite-plugin` . Run without arguments, it stops and asks for a directory. Per the[deploy docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cf/projects/) , one` cf deploy` call builds and checks the project, works out which credentials and account to use, then uploads a new Worker Version and makes it live. A static site needs no config file before its first` cf deploy` .


If your project has a wrangler.toml, wrangler.json or wrangler.jsonc, migrate it before you run` cf dev` ,` cf build` or` cf deploy` . Those three commands only look at cloudflare.config.ts and ignore any Wrangler config file.


```text
cf   migrate   --dry-run
cf   migrate
```


` cf migrate` reads TOML directly, so you don’t need to convert old files first. If you only want a JSON view of a legacy wrangler.toml, use a[TOML to JSON converter](https://openreplay.com/tools/toml-to-json/) . The cf for Wrangler users guide explains that migration sticks with Wrangler’s bundler unless the project already uses the Cloudflare Vite plugin, so moving to Vite is optional. When it keeps Wrangler’s bundler, it writes a` wrangler.config.ts` , and the[migration docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cf/wrangler/migrate/) say the Worker’s package needs Wrangler 4.136.0 or later installed. The launch post adds that Rust and Python Workers also keep delegating to Wrangler.


## What Happens to Wrangler?


Wrangler keeps working for now, but its end date is set. Once the cf open beta ends, Cloudflare plans to ship a final major Wrangler version that directs users to cf, then maintain Wrangler for 18 months from that point. Cloudflare hasn’t announced when the beta ends, so the 18 months has no calendar date yet.


Vite becoming the default build fits a wider move toward Vite in the Workers ecosystem.


## Conclusion


You can install cf alongside Wrangler: its resource commands run in an unmigrated project, and the switch only matters when you move a Worker’s builds onto it. Install the official package, run` cf zones list | jq .` to see the output for yourself, then test` cf migrate --dry-run` on a branch of a non-critical Worker before the beta ends and Wrangler’s maintenance period starts.


## FAQs


How do I use cf with more than one Cloudflare account?


Use named profiles. Run cf auth create work to create a profile and sign in to it, then cf auth activate work to link it to the current folder and every folder below it. Pass --profile work to use a profile for one command, and cf auth list to see all profiles. A CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN environment variable overrides every profile, and blocks profile management commands while set.


Can cf read credentials from a .env file?


Yes. API commands can pick up CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID and CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_ID from a .env file in the folder you run them from. cf only looks at .env, not .env.local, so make sure .env is listed in .gitignore. A token loaded this way takes priority over any profile or stored login. cf does not support the Global API Key, so use a scoped API token instead.


How do I migrate a Wrangler project inside a monorepo?


Pass the config file path to cf migrate, for example cf migrate packages/api/wrangler.jsonc --dry-run, then run the same command without --dry-run. Without a path, cf migrate expects exactly one wrangler.json, wrangler.jsonc or wrangler.toml in the current directory. It writes its files next to the config file, picks the bundler from package.json unless you pass --bundler vite or --bundler wrangler, and needs --force if the Git worktree is not clean.


What happens if I run cf deploy in a Wrangler project before migrating?


cf ignores wrangler.jsonc and wrangler.toml, so it can set the project up on its own and change files such as package.json. To recover, run git status, restore each changed file with git restore, and delete new files such as cloudflare.config.ts, wrangler.config.ts and the .cloudflare directory. Then run cf migrate, which does not run while a cloudflare.config.ts exists.
